docs.title: We start with this Winter Storm season, and then Fire later
docs.text:
Hoopa Valley Tribe • Columbia NCDP • Tribal Resilience Initiative

The initiative is a:

  • Co-designing sovereign text simulations for Hoopa Valley and neighboring Tribal Nations.
  • Twilio.org & Open-source tools built with Columbia University, National Center for Disaster Preparedness (NCDP) & Eugene Wu Lab (NSF Grant #2103794).

The project strengthens community readiness before severe winter weather strikes.

docs.title: Foundation & Governance
docs.text:
The project's foundation and governance are built on:

  • Tribal Data Ownership: ensuring that Tribes maintain full control over data storage, access, and deletion.
  • Open-Source Codebase: the platform uses an open-source codebase that is publicly adaptable via columbia-desdr.github.io.
  • Co-Design Team: Led through a close co-design partnership with Dan Osgood and RobRoy from Hoopa Valley Tribe.

docs.title: Regional Replication & GitHub Deployment
docs.text:
This framework is built to be adapted and self-hosted by neighboring Tribal Nations:

  • Multi-hazard ready: Customize the SMS scripts for wildfires, floods, or other regional emergencies.
  • Local landmarks & language: Utilize local road names, shelter locations, and Tribal audio recordings.
  • Inter-Tribal mutual aid: Share operational lessons across Yurok, Karuk, and neighboring communities.
  • Self-hosted on GitHub: Fork the open-source codebase and set up your own SMS phone line.

docs.title: Interactive Exercise: Four SMS Simulations
docs.text:
We will illustrate interactive two-way exercise for four categories of communications. Please think about which of these might be helpful from your perspective, and how you would set them up.

Step & Keyword Focus Area Function 01 • HVTstorm Storm Memory Paints the picture of past storm impacts at the Hoopa Valley Tribe. 02 • HVTalert Live Crisis Routing Branches rescues, sandbags, and volunteers during an active event. 03 • HVTsafe Discrete Discussions Surfaces unspoken evacuation barriers anonymously.

docs.title: Exercise 2: HVTalert--Going beyond one way alerts to ask questions
docs.text:
This is an example of a potential alert system, where instead of simply getting an alert, the community has a chance to provide feedback, or ask questions. During an active emergency, HVTalert could inform triage by routing residents based on their immediate situation.

Of course, this avenue depends on people having functioning networks to be workable, which is often a challenge during a disaster.

I need resources Specific resources needed, transport access Resource and staging dispatch 3. I have information or resources Wellness check, hazard report, community resource offer Verified situational map or volunteer pool

docs.title: Exercise 4: HVTcoordinate--Coordinating resources before and during disasters
docs.text:
For this illustration, we examine the setup of and needs for resources at three shelter facilities, with people role playing different roles. This could also be set up with non-hypothetical roles, locations and needs, informed by experts, reports, and community exercises like the ones we have already explored.

To align logistics across the entire community, HVTcoordinate runs three simultaneous tracks:

  • Track 1 (Residents): Maps household valley sectors, medical power dependencies, and endurance limits.
  • Track 2 (Providers): Audits facility generator fuel supplies and staffing bottlenecks.
  • Track 3 (Leadership): Evaluates central hub staging versus decentralized sector supply caches.

To start the activity, send by text or WhatsApp to

docs.text:
To end the activity at any time send #bye

The next page has the results.

  • What gaps do you see?

  • Where did the service get offered when needed?

  • How could you use this communications strategy before and during emergencies?

docs.title: Exercise 3: HVTsafe: Safe Space for Challenging Discussions
docs.text:
This is an example of an exercise to help in disaster preparedness through a safe space for challenging discussions.

Many discussions around disaster actions require sensitivity for people to feel safe describing their needs. For example Evacuation decisions are rarely simple. HVTsafe creates an anonymous space for residents to discuss tough household dilemmas—such as leaving animals behind, guarding homes, or caring for Elders. Using peer-mirror scoring, participants guess how their neighbors responded to help break feelings of isolation, while an anonymous community board surfaces practical solutions for Tribal planners.

(Note: Pilot exercise data exploring how household roles shape evacuation willingness is featured in the accompanying presentation charts.)

To start the activity, send

docs.title: HVTsafe by text or WhatsApp to +1 (646) 217-0881

The results of the activity are on the next page.

  • How could you use these approaches for disaster preparedness?

  • How hypothetical or playful would they be?

docs.title: Exercise 1: HVTstorm--Learning from Experts and the Community
docs.text:
This simulation is an example of gathering lived storm experiences from both residents and responders to identify real-world case studies and community needs to inform disaster preparedness and response

In this example, we ask two broad groups for their very different perspectives, community members who are served, and the teams that work to serve the community.

  • Community Experiences: Residents share past challenges—such as unreachable grocery stores, power loss, and missing emergency updates—alongside community support efforts like sharing firewood, shoveling driveways, and checking on neighbors on foot.
  • Responder Actions & Hazards: Government and Tribal responders document past actions (plowing, sanding roads, clearing trees, opening warming shelters) and recurring hazards like downed power lines, active mudslides, and black ice.

docs.title: The Communication Shift: From Broadcasting to Listening
docs.text:
Existing emergency systems rely on one-way alerts that broadcast information without knowing who actually needs help. But most communication devices, and many systems already in place can not only send, but can also recieve. There may be major benefits to using those technologies to shift the focus from broadcasting orders to listening by using thoughtful two-way SMS structured conversations that might be focused enough to work with limited cell signal

We want to discuss with you how you might be able to unlock opportunities using two way disaster communications.

One-Way Alerts (Already Exist) Two-Way SMS (New Opportunity) Zero feedback: Responders may not know who needs rescue. Community may not know what to do or where to go Live triage: Residents voice their own needs directly. Outside messengers: Generic alerts often face low local trust. Trusted and Trustworthy Tribal voice: Use local landmarks and Tribal protocols. Bandwidth heavy: Lots of extra searching for how and who to communicate with-Web links may fail during severe outages. 1-bar resilience: Thoughtful, pre-planned Plain SMS. Siloed systems: Tribal and state data can be disconnected. Shared picture: Connects Elders, field crews, and OES working together.

docs.title: Hoopa Valley Operational Reality
docs.text:
Emergency planning in Hoopa Valley must account for steep canyon geography and winter isolation:

  • Severed travel routes: Landslides and fallen trees frequently block Highway 96 and Bald Hills Road.
  • Extended power loss: Multi-day PG&E outages threaten home heating and critical medical oxygen devices.
  • Rural addressing: Many households rely on local landmarks and mile markers rather than standard street addresses.
